newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka soon to privatise more plantations.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka soon to privatise more plantations.

text.p: Sri Lanka will privatise more state plantation companies, which are expected to boost their performance on the back of strong tea and rubber prices, government and industry officials said on Friday.

Public Enterprises Reform Commission (PERC) officials said 51 percent stakes in six plantation management firms, categorised as loss-making ventures, would be sold to pre-qualified bidders starting in May.
Most of the firms, which are to be sold through the Colombo Stock Exchange, had accumulated debts of around 200 million rupees ($3.4 million) each, PERC officials said.
But Dr Anura Ekanayake, a director with the Plantation Industries Ministry, said a turnaround in tea and rubber prices has led to a resurgence of the plantation business.
"The plantations are now mostly running at a profit after losing money for several years," he told Reuters. "In most cases, high losses have come down."

The first three to be sold, Namunukula Plantations, Malwatta Valley Plantations and Maturata Plantations, posted pre-tax profits in the first nine months to September 1996, but the others, Kahawatte Plantations, Elpitiya Plantations and Elkaduwa Plantations, are still making a loss.
The government hopes to earn about 900 million rupees from sale of the first three firms, officials said.
Industry analysts said their performance was expected to improve.

"Buoyed by steep price increases in both tea and rubber, (the) plantation sector is poised to regain its lost glory" after several years of mismanagement under state control, said a report by UBS Global Research and John Keells Stock Brokers.
The industry had a future because private management had ploughed back money into replanting, fertilisers and machinery, while efforts have been made to cut costs and raise productivity, it said.

"Given current high tea and stable rubber prices, the government will be keen to conclude (privatisation) as soon as possible (hoping to get) high prices for the 51 percent controlling stakes," the report said.
The Indian Ocean island is privatising its tea, rubber and coconut plantations, once the bedrock of the economy. Foreign companies are not allowed to control more than 49 percent of the companies.
The government has sold 13 of its 23 plantation management firms which own some 600,000 hectares (1.5 million acres) of tea, rubber and coconut.

The six listed firms -- Bogawantalawa Plantations, Kotagala Plantations, Agalwatte Plantations, Kegalle Plantations, Horana Plantations, Kelani Valley Plantations -- saw their net profit rising between 50 percent and 500 percent in 1996.

Privatisation began in 1995 by selling 51 percent of the firms to a strategic investor and 20 percent to the public on the Colombo Stock Exchange. Ten percent was reserved for workers and the government retained the balance. ($1=Rs.58.68)
